entries.question: When are the problem sets due?
entries.answer: Each lecture has its own set on WeBWorK. The set for a Wednesday lecture is ps1 for that week and the set for the Saturday lecture is ps2; both open when they are published, before their lecture, and close at 23:59 on the Sunday of the week after their lectures, so there is always more than a full week to work on each. Attempts before the deadline are unlimited. Two copies of every set are linked beside the slides in the course plan below: a practice copy of the problems, and a solutions copy of the same problems worked through in full with an answer key at the end. Both carry their own randomly generated numbers, so the figures in them will not match your own copy on WeBWorK — which is the point. Follow the method, not the arithmetic.

entries.question: What is covered on 9 September?
entries.answer: 9 September: Course orientation. What statistics is: populations, samples, and the inferential problem. Describing a data set: frequency distributions and relative frequency histograms. Reading: Wackerly, Mathematical Statistics with Applications, 7th ed., §§1.1–1.2. Skim the Chapter 1 introduction before class.

entries.question: What is covered on 12 September?
entries.answer: 12 September: Numerical descriptive measures: the mean, the variance and the standard deviation. Tchebysheff's theorem and the empirical rule as distribution-free bounds. Why inference requires a measure of goodness. Reading: Wackerly §§1.3–1.6. Exercises at the end of §1.3, and the Chapter 1 supplementary exercises.

entries.question: What is covered on 16 September?
entries.answer: 16 September: The probability of an event: sample spaces, simple and compound events, set notation, and the three axioms. The sample-point method for discrete sample spaces. Reading: Wackerly §§2.1–2.5. Exercises at the end of §2.4.

entries.question: What is covered on 19 September?
entries.answer: 19 September: Tools for counting sample points: the mn rule, permutations, combinations, and partitions into groups. Sampling with and without replacement. Reading: Wackerly §2.6. Exercises at the end of §2.6.

entries.question: What is covered on 23 September?
entries.answer: 23 September: Conditional probability and the independence of events; independence contrasted with mutual exclusivity. Reading: Wackerly §2.7. Exercises at the end of §2.7.

entries.question: What is covered on 26 September?
entries.answer: 26 September: The additive and multiplicative laws of probability. Probabilities of unions, intersections and complements. Reading: Wackerly §2.8. Exercises at the end of §2.8. Tutorial week: TA-led tutorial this week.

entries.question: What is covered on 30 September?
entries.answer: 30 September: Calculating the probability of an event: the event-composition method. Extended worked problems on system reliability and compound financial events. Reading: Wackerly §2.9. Exercises at the end of §2.9.

entries.question: What is covered on 3 October?
entries.answer: 3 October: The law of total probability and Bayes' rule. Applications: credit screening, diagnostic testing, and the revision of prior beliefs in the light of evidence. Reading: Wackerly §2.10. Exercises at the end of §2.10.

entries.question: What is covered on 7 October?
entries.answer: 7 October: Numerical events and random variables: the passage from events to distributions. Chapter 2 synthesis and problem clinic. Reading: Wackerly §§2.11–2.13. Supplementary exercises, Chapter 2.

entries.question: What is covered on 10 October?
entries.answer: 10 October: Discrete random variables: the probability mass function and its properties. Expected value of a random variable and of a function of one; variance and standard deviation. Reading: Wackerly §§3.1–3.3. Exercises at the end of §3.3. Tutorial week: TA-led tutorial this week.

entries.question: What is covered on 14 October?
entries.answer: 14 October: The binomial distribution: derivation from Bernoulli trials, mean, variance, and use in counting defaults and defects. Reading: Wackerly §3.4. Exercises at the end of §3.4.

entries.question: What is covered on 17 October?
entries.answer: 17 October: Quiz I on WeBWorK, first 30 minutes of class (Chapters 1–2). The geometric and negative binomial distributions: waiting for the first success and for the rth success; memorylessness in discrete time. Reading: Prepare Wackerly Chapters 1–2 for the quiz. Reading for the lecture: §§3.5–3.6.

entries.question: What is covered on 21 October?
entries.answer: 21 October: The hypergeometric and Poisson distributions; the Poisson limit of the binomial. Review session for Midterm Examination I. Reading: Wackerly §§3.7–3.8. Supplementary exercises, Chapters 1–3 (§§3.1–3.8). Tutorial week: TA-led tutorial this week.

entries.question: What is covered on 24 October?
entries.answer: 24 October: Midterm Examination I on WeBWorK — Chapters 1–3 (§§3.1–3.8), written during the regular class period of each section. Reading: Wackerly Chapters 1–2 and §§3.1–3.8. Bring a charged laptop. Statistical tables and a formula sheet are built into the WeBWorK set.

entries.question: What is covered on 28 October?
entries.answer: 28 October: Moments and moment-generating functions of discrete random variables; recovering the moments of a distribution by differentiation. Reading: Wackerly §3.9. Exercises at the end of §3.9.

entries.question: What is covered on 31 October?
entries.answer: 31 October: Probability-generating functions. Tchebysheff's theorem for discrete random variables. Chapter 3 synthesis: choosing among the discrete models. Reading: Wackerly §§3.10–3.11. Supplementary exercises, Chapter 3.

entries.question: What is covered on 4 November?
entries.answer: 4 November: Continuous random variables: the distribution function and the density function; the probability of an interval as an area under the density. Reading: Wackerly §§4.1–4.2. Exercises at the end of §4.2.

entries.question: What is covered on 7 November?
entries.answer: 7 November: Expected values for continuous random variables. The uniform distribution and its role as a reference model. Reading: Wackerly §§4.3–4.4. Exercises at the end of §§4.3–4.4. Tutorial week: TA-led tutorial this week.

entries.question: What is covered on 11 November?
entries.answer: 11 November: The normal distribution: shape, standardisation, use of the normal tables, and its place in the modelling of asset returns. Reading: Wackerly §4.5. Exercises at the end of §4.5.

entries.question: What is covered on 14 November?
entries.answer: 14 November: The gamma family: the gamma, exponential and chi-square distributions. Waiting times and lifetimes; the memoryless property in continuous time. Reading: Wackerly §4.6. Exercises at the end of §4.6.

entries.question: What is covered on 18 November?
entries.answer: 18 November: The beta distribution as a model for proportions. Choosing among the continuous models: general comments and comparisons. Reading: Wackerly §§4.7–4.8. Exercises at the end of §4.7.

entries.question: What is covered on 21 November?
entries.answer: 21 November: Moment-generating functions for continuous random variables; Tchebysheff's theorem; expectations of discontinuous functions. Chapter 4 synthesis. Reading: Wackerly §§4.9–4.11. Supplementary exercises, Chapter 4. Tutorial week: TA-led tutorial this week.

entries.question: What is covered on 25 November?
entries.answer: 25 November: Multivariate probability distributions: joint distribution functions and joint densities for the discrete and the continuous case. Reading: Wackerly §§5.1–5.2. Exercises at the end of §5.2.

entries.question: What is covered on 28 November?
entries.answer: 28 November: Marginal and conditional distributions: recovering one variable's behaviour from the joint law, and conditioning on the other. Reading: Wackerly §5.3. Exercises at the end of §5.3.

entries.question: What is covered on 2 December?
entries.answer: 2 December: Independent random variables: the factorisation criterion, and the ways independence fails in economic data. Reading: Wackerly §5.4. Exercises at the end of §5.4.

entries.question: What is covered on 5 December?
entries.answer: 5 December: The expected value of a function of several random variables. Covariance: definition, computation, and interpretation as co-movement. Reading: Wackerly §§5.5–5.7. Exercises at the end of §§5.5–5.7. Tutorial week: TA-led tutorial this week.

entries.question: What is covered on 9 December?
entries.answer: 9 December: The mean and variance of a linear combination of random variables; the variance of a two-asset portfolio and the arithmetic of diversification. Reading: Wackerly §5.8. Exercises at the end of §5.8.

entries.question: What is covered on 12 December?
entries.answer: 12 December: Quiz II on WeBWorK, first 30 minutes of class (Chapter 4 and §§5.1–5.8). The multinomial distribution. Reading: Prepare Wackerly Chapter 4 and §§5.1–5.8 for the quiz. Reading for the lecture: §5.9.

entries.question: What is covered on 16 December?
entries.answer: 16 December: The bivariate normal distribution. Conditional expectations and the regression function; the law of iterated expectations and the conditional-variance decomposition. Reading: Wackerly §§5.10–5.11. Exercises at the end of §5.11. Tutorial week: TA-led tutorial this week.

entries.question: What is covered on 19 December?
entries.answer: 19 December: Chapter 5 synthesis and comprehensive review of Chapters 1–5 in preparation for Midterm Examination II. Reading: Wackerly §5.12. Supplementary exercises, Chapter 5.

entries.question: What is covered on 23 December?
entries.answer: 23 December: Midterm Examination II on WeBWorK — comprehensive over Chapters 1–5, with emphasis on Chapters 4–5, written during the regular class period of each section. Reading: Wackerly Chapters 1–5, with emphasis on Chapters 4–5. Bring a charged laptop. Statistical tables and a formula sheet are built into the WeBWorK set.

entries.question: Blackboard Learn?
entries.answer: The single point of distribution for the course: slides after each session, problem set announcements and deadlines, and all grades through the Grade Centre. Check the course page before each session.

entries.question: WeBWorK?
entries.answer: Carries both practice and assessment. Access is arranged during the first week of classes. Bring a charged laptop to every quiz and examination.

entries.question: Tutorials?
entries.answer: Seven working sessions in alternate weeks, run by the teaching assistant. Day, time and room are announced on Blackboard in the first week.

entries.question: Contact?
entries.answer: Individual questions by e-mail to sorujov@ada.edu.az, answered within 48 hours on working days. Office hours Wednesday 16:00-18:00, Building D, Room D325.

entries.question: Attendance and grading?
entries.answer: Attendance follows chapter 6.3 of the University's Student Assessment Regulations; grading follows chapters 6.4 to 6.6. Grading rubrics are provided with each graded assignment.

entries.question: Academic integrity?
entries.answer: Full compliance with the principle of academic integrity is expected. Breaches are handled under the University's Honor Code, and grievances under the Student Academic Grievance Policy.

entries.question: What is the required reading?
entries.answer: Wackerly, D. D., Mendenhall, W. and Scheaffer, R. L. (2008). Mathematical Statistics with Applications, 7th edition. Brooks/Cole, Cengage Learning. The course follows Chapters 1 to 5 closely; the statistical tables in the appendix are the tables used in class.

entries.question: What is the recommended reading?
entries.answer: Casella, G. and Berger, R. L. (2002). Statistical Inference, 2nd edition, Chapters 1-4 — for students who want a more demanding treatment. Ross, S. M. (2019). A First Course in Probability, 10th edition — a gentler source of worked examples on combinatorics and conditional probability. Hogg, McKean and Craig (2019). Introduction to Mathematical Statistics, 8th edition — a second exposition of multivariate distributions.
